newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Firm US Sep CPI gains seen after soft Aug.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Firm US Sep CPI gains seen after soft Aug.

text.p: After an encouragingly meager rise in August, overall consumer prices likely advanced at a more rapid rate in September, boosted by higher apparel and airline prices, economists said on Tuesday.

However, because of the benign August figures, U.S. markets are prepared for a decent comeback in September and are unlikely to worry excessively about inflation before additional signs of price gains materialize.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics is scheduled to release the September CPI report at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Wednesday.

"People will average the two months together and still come up with a relatively benign inflation picture," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "It would take a consistent string of inflation numbers to persuade people that inflation is heading higher."
Economists surveyed by Reuters are expecting a firm 0.3 percent gain in September consumer prices versus a 0.1 percent advance in August.
The core reading, which excludes the volatile food and energy sectors, is also seen advancing at a 0.3 percent clip against a 0.1 percent gain in the previous month.

The Labor Department indicated last week that apparel prices may have been held down in August by the late introduction of fall fashions. Higher prices for new fashions should come through in the September release.
"The weakness we saw in apparel prices last month should reverse," said David Sloan, economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc, whose forecasts are exactly in line with consensus.
"Also, the reintroduction of an airline tax could boost the airfares a bit," he said.
Sloan said a 0.4 percent gain in the core reading for September could create some jitters in the markets but predicted figures below that threshold would be easily digested.

Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp, sees transportation, apparel, housing and services all contributing to the gains in September, setting the stage for a steady increase in consumer prices in the months ahead.
"We do think it is the beginning of more consistently strong CPI inflation over the next six months or so," said Liro.
He also expects the market to digest a September bounceback without difficulty. However, an additional strong reading for the month of October would get people's attention, he said.
"If we get to mid-November and see another 0.3 or 0.4 percent increase the day after the FOMC meeting, then I think the market will have a little bit more of a problem."
The October consumer price data will be released on the day after the Federal Reserve's upcoming November 13 meeting.
